title: Google Business Profile for Contractors: Setup Checklist
summary: Google Business Profile checklist for contractors: service area, categories, hours, phone, and reviews so listing calls get answered.
body_markdown:
A Google Business Profile is often the first place a homeowner sees your company name, your rating, and the Call button. For contractors, setup is not a one-time form. It is the map pin, the service area, the categories, the hours, the number on the listing, and the proof that you do the work you claim.


Most setup guides stop when the profile goes live. This one assumes you want calls. A profile that ranks but rings voicemail still loses the job. If you run[Google Local Services](https://sameday.ai/integration/google-local-services) , the same hours and phone number also set when a missed call can bill as a lead. The rules are in[Google LSA missed-call charges](https://sameday.ai/post/google-lsa-missed-call-charges) .


Marketplace and software choices sit on other pages:[Thumbtack vs Angi](https://sameday.ai/post/thumbtack-vs-angi) ,[virtual assistant for contractors](https://sameday.ai/post/virtual-assistant-for-contractors) , and[restoration software](https://sameday.ai/post/restoration-software) .


## Service-area setup worksheet


Service-area businesses travel to the customer. Google's[Guidelines for representing your business on Google](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3038177) and[Add or edit your business address](https://support.google.com/business/answer/9157481) describe service-area setup, including when a street address must stay visible for hybrid storefront locations. Work through the list before you publish.


Nine steps before you publish a contractor profile


1.


Claim or create the profile


Use the Google account that will own verification. Google's[Add or claim your Business Profile](https://support.google.com/business/answer/2911778) page walks through claim, duplicate, and ownership disputes.


2.


Choose service area or storefront


If customers are served at home with no public storefront, register as a service-area business and hide the street address, per Google's service-area rules. If you operate a hybrid location where customers walk in, keep the address visible.


3.


Draw realistic zones


List cities or ZIP codes you can reach with normal dispatch—not every adjacent county for visibility. Remove areas where you routinely decline jobs.


4.


Match Local Services coverage


If you advertise on Local Services, service areas and categories should match what a tech can actually run tomorrow.


5.


Set the primary category


Pick the one category that best describes your core trade. Add secondary categories only for services you book regularly.


6.


Use your real business name


Google's guidelines prohibit extra keywords in the name field. The sign on your truck is the name; "HVAC - Plumbing - 24/7" is not.


7.


Publish hours someone answers


Set hours to your real operating schedule—the days and times you dispatch crews or book new jobs. Route after-hours calls through your phone or answering setup; do not mark the profile 24/7 unless you truly operate that way.


8.


Assign the main phone number


Use the number that should ring for new customers. Call-tracking numbers are fine only when your business controls the line directly—not a provider-owned pool you do not control—and it forwards to Sameday or your answering setup.


9.


Add photos and services


Upload recent job, team, and vehicle shots. Fill service items you want to appear for when Google shows them on the profile.


After Google verifies the profile and the listing appears on Search or Maps, place a test call from a phone that is not saved as staff. Tap Call on the listing during business hours and again after hours, and note what rings. Keep those notes as the baseline before you spend on ads or marketplaces.


## What influences local rankings


Google does not publish a full local ranking formula. Its help material still groups local results around relevance, distance, and prominence. For contractors, that usually means the right categories, a clear service area, consistent business information, reviews, photos, and engagement on the profile.


Factor What to do on the profile Why it matters for calls


Relevance Primary and secondary categories that match the jobs you book; accurate services; business description in plain language. The listing should appear for the trade the homeowner searched, not a near match you decline.


Distance Service area drawn to cities and ZIPs you actually dispatch; remove dead zones. Service area sets where Google may show the listing; it does not guarantee every nearby searcher sees you.


Prominence Steady review flow, owner responses, fresh photos, updated hours, and a working website link. Homeowners compare ratings and recent activity before they tap Call.


Consistency Same business name, address or service-area setup, and phone on the site, trucks, and invoices. Mismatches create duplicate listings and wrong numbers on the Knowledge Panel.


Engagement Answer Q&A, post occasional updates, and use messaging only if you monitor it. Quiet or wrong Q&A pushes callers to the next contractor in the pack.


Ranking is only visibility. Conversion is whether someone answers the tap on Call.


## Business name and categories


Google's guidelines say your name should match your real-world signage and branding. Keyword stuffing in the name field—city names, trade lists, or marketing slogans—is a policy issue and a common suspension trigger. Put specialties in categories and services, not in the title.


### HVAC contractors


Use a primary category such as HVAC contractor or air conditioning contractor, then add heating and related categories only if you take those calls. Seasonal demand means wrong categories send tune-up traffic to a shop that only sells install, or emergency heat calls to a maintenance-only line.


### Plumbers


Plumber is the usual primary category; add drain, water heater, or sewer categories when those crews are on your board. If you subcontract gas line work, say so in services and on the phone, not with a misleading category.


### Roofers


Roofing contractor fits most shingle and metal work. Storm response companies often add categories for inspection or repair only when that work is dispatched in-house. Insurance-heavy shops still need a number that answers when adjusters and homeowners call from the profile.


When you change categories, watch the Local Services vertical tied to the profile. A category shift can change which jobs qualify for Local Services until Google re-verifies the account.


## Hours, phone, and Local Services


Business hours on the profile are what many homeowners trust for "open now." They are also the hours Google uses for some Local Services missed-call rules. Google's[How leads work](https://support.google.com/localservices/answer/7195435) page states that business hours are the hours you set in your Google Business Profile, and that a missed phone call during those hours can be charged when the caller stays on the line for more than twenty seconds.


For service-area businesses without a walk-in location, set hours to when you actually operate and dispatch—not only when the shop door is unlocked. If dispatch goes home at five but you still sell emergency plumbing, keep published hours accurate and use call routing or after-hours answering for overnight coverage.


The profile phone should be the number you want on new jobs. If it forwards to a tracking pool, test the whole chain: listing tap, forward, hold music, voicemail, and after-hours path. Voicemail during business hours can still count as a connected call under Google's Local Services rules when the caller waits long enough. Details are on[Google LSA missed-call charges](https://sameday.ai/post/google-lsa-missed-call-charges) .


Special hours matter after storms and holidays. Google's[How to set Special hours](https://support.google.com/business/answer/6303076) flow lets you mark closures or extended emergency coverage without editing the regular week template every time.


## Reviews


Reviews are a prominence signal and a trust filter before the call. Google allows you to ask customers for feedback. Google's[Prohibited & restricted content](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3474122) policies forbid review gating and prohibit incentives for reviews at any star rating, including paying or discounting only when someone leaves a review.


A steady process beats a burst after one big job:


- Ask after the work is complete, with a direct link to your profile review form.
- Reply to new reviews with specifics, not boilerplate thanks.
- Flag policy violations through Google's tools when a review is clearly off-topic or spam; do not argue in public on questionable posts.
- Fix the operational issue when the same complaint repeats; ratings follow operations.


Reviews attract the call. They do not book the job if nobody picks up.


## Photos and profile completeness


Google's[Add photos & videos](https://support.google.com/business/answer/6103862) guidance recommends images that show the business, team, and work. For contractors, useful sets usually include:


- Branded trucks or vans at completed jobs
- Technicians in uniform, with safety gear appropriate to the trade
- Before-and-after shots you have permission to publish
- Office or shop only if customers actually visit


Replace stale hero images after fleet rebrands or uniform changes. Profiles with recent photos look active next to competitors with dated galleries.


Add services and products when Google offers the fields for your category. Keep descriptions short and literal. Link to your site only if the booking path on that page matches what callers hear on the phone.

Setup gets the listing right. Sameday handles what happens when Call connects.


What Sameday does with a profile-driven call


On the call


Answer, qualify, book


24/7, including after hours and spikes. Qualified jobs can land on the board during the conversation.


Then


If it does not connect


Call and text back

Sameday answers when the Google Business Profile number rings into your setup. Local Services ad calls follow the phone number configured in your Local Services account, which can differ from the profile—check that routing separately so paid leads do not bypass Sameday. ## FAQ


### Is a Google Business Profile free for contractors?


Google says you can add or claim your Business Profile at no charge. The listing still needs accurate hours, a working phone number, and categories that match what you do.


### Should contractors hide their address on Google?


Service-area businesses without a public storefront must hide the street address and define a service area. Hybrid storefront locations keep the address visible. Google requires that you serve customers at their locations and follow its service-area guidelines.


### How many categories can a contractor add?


Google lets you choose a primary category and additional categories that describe your services. Pick categories that match real work; Google's help pages warn against categories that do not fit the business.


### Do Google Business Profile hours affect Local Services Ads?


Yes for missed-call billing. Google's Local Services help says business hours are the hours you set in your Google Business Profile, and unanswered calls during those hours can be charged when other valid-lead rules apply.


### Can contractors ask customers for Google reviews?


Google allows you to ask customers for reviews. Google's policies prohibit review gating and incentives for reviews at any star rating, including paying or discounting only when someone leaves a review.


### Does Sameday answer calls from a Google Business Profile?


Yes, on the lines you route. Sameday answers when the profile number or your Local Services account's configured number rings in; confirm Local Services call routing in that account, not only on the profile. Sameday can answer 24/7, qualify the job, and book into ServiceTitan or Housecall Pro during the call.


Sources:[Guidelines for representing your business on Google](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3038177) and[Prohibited & restricted content](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3474122) (reviews).
